title: The New Chinese Way of Cyberwar
gist: Former Deputy U.S. National Security Adviser Anne Neuberger argues that digital chokepoints are as dangerous as physical ones: Chinese hackers have pre-positioned inside U.S. communications, energy and transportation infrastructure to enable sabotage, much as Iran has weaponized the Strait of Hormuz. Only the opening of the paywalled essay is available.

insights.claim: Markets and policymakers have focused on physical economic chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz and critical minerals, while chokepoints in the digital domain are underappreciated yet could prove just as treacherous.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Cyber-sabotage risk to infrastructure is likely under-priced relative to commodity chokepoint risk; watch cybersecurity and critical-infrastructure resilience spending.
insights.quote: Less consideration, however, has been paid to chokepoints in the digital domain, which could prove just as treacherous.

insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Chokepoint coercion is now an active tool of statecraft; supply-chain concentration is a live geopolitical risk factor, not a tail risk.

insights.claim: Chinese hackers have gained and retained access to U.S. communications, energy and transportation infrastructure, and the purpose of these intrusions is to lay the groundwork for sabotage rather than only to gather intelligence.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: A U.S.-China crisis could bring disruptive attacks on utilities, telecoms and logistics; favors grid/OT security vendors and raises operational risk for infrastructure operators.

insights.claim: Beijing is expected to weaponize digital chokepoints in the same way Iran has used the Strait of Hormuz, turning persistent network access into coercive leverage.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Treat cyber access as a bargaining chip in U.S.-China negotiations; escalation episodes may feature infrastructure disruption threats.
